title: Detection of Object-Recognition Impairment in Alzheimer’s Disease
summary:
Memory performance declines with increasing age. Today, it is possible to determine with great accuracy whether or not Alzheimer's disease is the cause of memory impairment.
However, it is also known that cognitive impairment progresses at different rates in different patients, making it difficult to predict how the symptoms will evolve based on the mere presence of Alzheimer's disease.

The spread Alzheimer's disease pathology in the brain typically follows a characteristic pattern. Memory-forming structures are initially affected, while the cerebral cortex is affected later in the course oft he disease. Involvement of the cerebral cortex is generally associated with greater impairment and more rapid decline than degeneration of memory-forming structures alone. Early detection of cortical involvement could therefore help to improve prognostic accuracy. Brain anatomy, in conjunction with the typical progression pattern of Alzheimer's disease, suggests that early cortical involvement should entail impairments of object recognition. While these are usually only noticed in late stages of the disease, they have not typically been specifically tested in the early stages.

The aim of this study is to determine the frequency of object recognition impairments in patients with memory impairment and early Alzheimer's disease and to investigate whether this can be used to predict disease progression.

interventions.name: Systematic assessment of impairment of object recognition and object memory in addition to the routine clinical diagnostics using the VOSP and a computer-based test at baseline and after a follow-up period of 9 to 12 months.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
• Presentation to a memory clinic due to memory problems reported by the patient or others
• Impaired memory performance, assessed using standardized neuropsychological tests
• (corrected) adequate vision and hearing, as well as adequate language skills (prerequisite for a differentiated neuropsychological examination)
Exclusion criteria:
• Serious pre-existing medical conditions as potential causes of memory impairment (e.g., schizophrenia, psychosis, severe depressive episode, mania, personality disorders, territorial cerebral ischemia, cerebral ischemia with residual deficit, epilepsy, Parkinson's syndrome, history of whole-brain irradiation, cerebrospinal fluid circulation disorders, acute or chronic CNS disease, intracranial malignancies, alcohol or drug addiction)
• Inability to give informed consent
